title: Domains: registration, DNS, propagation and subdomains

videos.script: Every lesson so far has started after the address was known. A packet goes to a number; a request goes to a machine; a cookie comes back to a name. None of them said where the number came from. {{so-far}} You typed a name. Machines do not use names. Something between the two has to happen, and it happens before a single byte of your request has been sent. {{gap}} That something is the largest database in the world, and it has no centre. {{no-centre}} Nobody holds the list. There is no file anywhere with every domain in it. Instead there is a chain of servers, each of which knows one thing: who to ask next. {{chain}} Your machine asks a resolver. The resolver asks the root, which says ask the one who runs dot com. That one says ask the one who runs this domain. And that one, finally, answers with a number. {{four-steps}} Four questions, and only the last one actually knows. {{last-one}} By the end of this lesson you will be able to say what you actually bought when you bought a domain, why a change takes hours to show up, why it takes hours for some people and not others, and which of the half-dozen record types answers the question you have. {{title}}

One domain, and everything a small company needs, pointed at four different places. Start with what we hold. {{hold}} We bought example dot com. That gives us this name and every name underneath it, for nothing further — no purchase, no approval, no waiting. A subdomain is a line in a file we already control. {{free}} So. The site itself goes to the hosting provider. One record, a name to an address. {{www}} The application is somewhere else — a different provider, a different address. app dot example dot com, a second record, and nothing about the first one changed. {{app}} Now the mail. This is the one people get wrong, so watch the type. Mail is not an address record. It is an MX, and it names a server rather than a number, with a priority in front of it. Point it at whoever runs the mailboxes. {{mx}} And the documentation, which lives on a service that gives us a name rather than an address. That is a CNAME: this name is an alias for that name, go and ask again. {{cname}} Four records, four destinations, one domain. And here is the part that matters for the rest of your working life. {{four}} Nothing here is your server. Each of these is a line saying where to go, and the lines cost nothing to change. Moving a site between providers is editing one of them. {{lines}} The waiting is the only real cost, and you met it in the reading: it is not propagation, it is the TTL you set yourself, running out. Lower it the day before you move, and the move takes minutes instead of a day. {{ttl}}
